pr_title: fix(core): ensure sanitizer works if DOMParser return null body
pr_body:
In some browsers, notably a mobile version of webkit on iPad, the
result of calling `DOMParser.parseFromString()` returns a document
whose `body` property is null until the next tick of the browser.
Since this is of no use to us for sanitization, we now fall back to the
"inert document" strategy for this case.

Fixes #39834
pr_comments: @koto can you take a look too?
From a security point of view, I want to know whether there are situations where the inert document helper should not be used even if the DOMParser helper fails...

> From a security point of view, I want to know whether there are situations where the inert document helper should not be used even if the DOMParser helper fails...

Not to my knowledge. LGTM.
@petebacondarwin This fix is amazing. Thank you. It reduced my exception metric by 90%... seriously.

review_comments:
I am a bit confused as #39834 reports a crash at the call site of this method:

https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/3e1e5a15ba1d5a08daf9179083e3394df10299bb/packages/core/src/sanitization/html_sanitizer.ts#L267

which is strange as I'd have expected the `body.removeChild(body.firstChild)` below to have crashed instead if `body` is in fact `null`.

---

After typing the above I realized that it's the `catch` clause below that introduces the `null`, which is how the code mentioned before crashes. So I don't think that the fix as is would actually address the issue.

There are actually two `null`s :-)

The first is the `body` property on the document returned from `parseFromString()`. This causes an exception when accessing `body.removeChild()`, which we catch and then convert to another `null`, which is returned. This `null` is then assigned to `inertBodyElement`, which causes another exception, when we try to access `inertBodyElement.innerHTML`.

So avoiding that first `body===null` solves the problem, I believe. 
Hopefully @jsgoupil can try this out with his site and see if it does indeed solve the problem.
I looked at the code and it seems to fix it. I had bypassed the whole DOMParserHelper and I was not experiencing any issues.
Notably, if I remove the "fix" then the test I added does indeed fail with the exception given in the original error report.

Ah, that makes sense. The catch clause is still a potential source of `null`, but at least this cause is now prevented. I am wondering if the fallback strategy should also be used in the case of an error (although I do share your concern of falling back to a different strategy even if `DOMParser` is available)
Falling back for random exceptions from the DOMParser is definitely too risky IMO.

Yes I think that's fair. So that would mean that this non-null assertion remains a potential crash:

https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/3e1e5a15ba1d5a08daf9179083e3394df10299bb/packages/core/src/sanitization/html_sanitizer.ts#L267
